steps.tx: A **target cell**, designated scientifically as a codocyte or Mexican hat cell, represents an abnormal erythrocyte characterized by a central rounded area of hemoglobin surrounded by a clear concentric halo and an outer hemoglobinized rim. The pathognomonic biophysical defect responsible for target cell formation is an increased surface-area-to-volume ratio of the red blood cell.
steps.say: Target cells, or codocytes, look like miniature archery targets or Mexican hats on blood films. They feature a central bullseye of pink hemoglobin, surrounded by a clear ring, enclosed by an outer pink rim. This distinctive look occurs whenever the red blood cell has an increased surface area relative to its internal volume.

vis.alt: Peripheral blood smear displaying target cells and sickle cells under high power magnification.
vis.caption: Target cells displaying central hemoglobin disc and outer peripheral rim on blood smear.

steps.tx: An increased surface-to-volume ratio arises through two distinct physiological mechanisms: **absolute membrane excess** or decreased intracellular hemoglobin content. Absolute membrane expansion occurs when excess cholesterol and phospholipids incorporate into the lipid bilayer, as seen in obstructive liver disease. Conversely, decreased cytoplasmic volume occurs when defective globin chain or heme synthesis produces underfilled, microcytic hypochromic cells.
steps.say: Target cells form through two main pathways: too much membrane or too little hemoglobin. In obstructive jaundice, excess cholesterol piles into the outer cell membrane, making it floppy. In thalassaemias and severe iron deficiency, the cell lacks hemoglobin, so the normal membrane droops like a deflated balloon.

steps.tx: In severe hemoglobinopathies, **haemoglobin C disease** produces the highest percentage of target cells, often exceeding forty to fifty percent of all circulating erythrocytes. Hemoglobin C results from a point mutation at codon six substituting lysine for glutamic acid. The mutant hemoglobin has low aqueous solubility, precipitating into dense rod-shaped or hexagonal intraerythrocytic crystals that force residual hemoglobin into a central bullseye target.
steps.say: Hemoglobin C disease produces more target cells than almost any other condition, often over forty percent of the smear. A point mutation substitutes lysine for glutamic acid. Hemoglobin C crystallizes easily into hexagonal, rod-shaped crystals inside the cell, leaving behind classic, rigid target cells.

left.title: Haemoglobin C Disease (HbCC)
points: Lysine substituted at codon 6 of beta chain

right.title: Thalassaemia Major / Minor
points: Severe hypochromia with low MCV (<70 fL)

steps.tx: In liver disease, target cell genesis is driven by **lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase** (LCAT) deficiency. Biliary obstruction elevates circulating unesterified cholesterol and bile salts, which inhibit LCAT activity. Excess free cholesterol and phosphatidylcholine transfer directly from plasma lipoproteins into the erythrocyte outer leaflet. The surface area expands by up to twenty percent without any change in cell volume, buckling the central membrane.
steps.say: In obstructive liver disease, bile stasis shuts down the enzyme LCAT. Unesterified free cholesterol in plasma transfers directly into the red cell outer membrane, expanding its surface area by twenty percent. The floppy excess membrane folds into the center, creating macrocytic target cells.

left.title: Liver Disease Target Cells
points: LCAT enzyme inhibition by biliary obstruction
Direct lipid transfer expands outer membrane
Cells are macrocytic or normocytic (high MCV)

steps.tx: The critical diagnostic pitfall is confusing target cells with **stomatocytes or artefacts**. True target cells display symmetric concentric rings across the entire smear, whereas drying artefacts exhibit irregular off-center puddles. Splenectomy universally increases target cells because the spleen normally conditions erythrocytes, plucking out redundant lipid. Target cells possess increased osmotic resistance, shifting the osmotic fragility curve to the left.
steps.say: Be careful not to confuse real target cells with drying artefacts. True target cells show crisp concentric rings throughout the film. Remember that target cells have excess membrane, making them unusually resistant to bursting in hypotonic water, which shifts the osmotic fragility curve to the left, the exact opposite of spherocytes.

quiz.q: What is the primary biophysical abnormality responsible for target cell (codocyte) formation?
quiz.explain: Target cells form due to an increased surface-area-to-volume ratio, caused either by absolute membrane lipid excess or by decreased intracellular hemoglobin content.

quiz.q: How does the presence of target cells affect the red blood cell osmotic fragility curve?
options: Shifts the curve to the left, indicating increased resistance to osmotic lysis
Shifts the curve to the right, indicating premature lysis in hypotonic saline
Has zero effect on osmotic fragility parameters
Causes immediate instantaneous lysis in isotonic saline
quiz.explain: Because target cells have redundant surface membrane, they can take up more water before their membrane stretches to the lytic threshold, shifting the curve to the left (decreased fragility).
